title: Kernel blending strategy + KV-coherence scratchpad
summary: Working notes for a blended-kernel runtime approach that mixes TensorRT, Triton-managed models, and custom CUDA kernels while keeping KV cache coherence and predictable SLOs. Focus: heuristics for kernel selection, KV cache ownership, memory residency, and fallback cost sensitivity.
body:
Purpose and context:
This is a working scratchpad capturing experiments and design options for blending kernel backends (TensorRT engines, Triton model instances, and hand-written CUDA kernels) in the serving runtime. Goal: keep latency SLOs stable while optimizing for unit cost and avoiding KV-cache thrashing across backend boundaries.

Problem statement (concise):
- Multiple kernel backends are available with different latency/cost profiles and memory footprints.
- KV cache (key-value attention cache) is a scarce large-memory resource; cross-backend eviction or copies can blow tail latency.
- Fallbacks (e.g., to CPU or lower-fidelity quantized engines) must not invalidate KV cache assumptions or cause excessive warmup stalls.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- Target SLOs: 50ms p50 and 150ms p99 for typical chat workloads (seq len <= 1024).
- GPU memory budgets vary: Dedicated nodes (A100-80GB), burst nodes (A10/RTX), and Triton-hosted instances (8–24GB).
- Models support both TensorRT serialized engines and Triton protobuf graph runtimes; custom kernels used for fused attention and rotary + kv-compact ops.

Design options explored (high level):
1) Unified ownership: single backend owns the KV cache for a request life-cycle. If request switches backend, either copy KV into target backend's memory or invalidate and recompute.
   - Pros: simple correctness model.
   - Cons: copy cost or recompute latency expensive for long contexts.
2) Shared pinned host-backed KV representation with lightweight device views per backend. Backends map the host KV without full copy (pinned page-locked memory + direct-GPU access).
   - Pros: avoids full device copies; faster backend switch.
   - Cons: requires page-locking budget and careful NUMA/GPU bus considerations; adds variance.
3) Split-KV by prefix: keep last-k tokens in device-local caches, offload older prefixes to compressed host cache. On backend switches, only copying a small tail window.
   - Pros: lower copy sizes, predictable worst-case.
   - Cons: additional logic for cache promotion, potential quality impact if old context is pruned incorrectly.

Kernel selection heuristics tested:
- Cost-aware latency-first: choose fastest backend if it fits memory + expected batch. Fallback to cheaper backend under high load.
- KV-affinity: prefer backend that already has a warm KV for that conversation (sticky routing for N tokens after last access).
- Sequence-aware multiplexing: when seq_len distribution skewed (many short, few long) route long sequences to high-memory backends, short ones to dense, cheap kernels.

Microbenchmarks (setup):
- Workloads: chat-sim (median turn 48 tokens), long-history chat (context 2048 tokens simulated by warmup), streaming-decoding (token-by-token).
- Backends: TRT-ENG (FP16 serialized, 1 beam), TRITON-VM (graph, dynamic batch), CUSTOM-FUSED (handwritten CUDA for attention + rotary).
- Metrics: token p50/p95/p99 latency, full-request latency, cost-per-1000-tokens (normalized), KV-copy bytes, memory high-water mark, SLO-violation rate.

Notable experimental outcomes (raw observations):
- Pure TRT engines deliver lowest per-token latency for steady-state decoding once KV in device memory; cold startup (first 2 tokens) often slower due to context upload.
- Triton graph instances have more consistent warmup behavior for small GPUs due to streaming-friendly buffer reuse but slightly worse steady-state per-token latency vs TRT on A100.
- Custom fused kernels reduce per-token latency for long-seq workloads where attention dominates CPU–GPU transfers, but they increase code-complexity and make fallbacks brittle.
- Host-pinned shared KV reduced cross-backend switch cost by ~3–6x vs full device copy in our tests, but increased p99 variance on noisy multi-tenant nodes.

Tradeoffs and recommended hybrid policy (current working proposal):
1) Maintain KV-affinity windows: after a request uses backend X, subsequent turns for that conversation are preferred to continue on X for up to M tokens or T seconds, whichever first. Default M=512 tokens, T=30s.
2) For backend switches, prefer delta-copy (copy only tail window of last W tokens) where W = min(256, current_seq_len). Server-side logic will reconstruct earlier context logically (offload compressed prefixes).
3) Keep a small host-pinned shared KV region for low-latency backend-to-backend views (configurable per-node; default 12GB pinned for dedicated hosts).
4) Prioritize TRT engines for steady-state decoding on high-memory nodes; route to Triton or custom fused on small GPUs or during burst to control cost.
5) Explicitly ban CPU fallback unless device memory pressure > 95% and request SLO is soft. CPU fallback triggers a synchronous client-side warning header so app can degrade UX.

Open questions / risks:
- NUMA and PCIe contention: pinned-host KV helped in some nodes but p99 worsened on nodes with shared NVLink; need cluster-level benchmarks.
- Security/isolation: host-pinned KV must be zeroed and deallocated per-tenant to avoid cross-tenant leakage; implementation needs CAS-based ownership guarantees.
- Consistency across model versions: when we serve model-variants (quantized vs full), KV representations differ; conversion cost may be non-trivial.
- Cost accounting: how to bill for pinned memory used for cross-backend views? Billing vs tenant isolation policy needed.

Experiment matrix (next steps):
- Run controlled A/B across 3 node types (80GB A100, 40GB A30, 24GB V100-equiv) with traffic mirrors of production for 72h window.
- Variables: KV-policy (full copy / delta / pinned), Kernel mix (TRT-primary / Triton-primary / Custom-primary), Affinity window sizes (128/256/512).
- Primary KPIs: p99 latency, SLO violation rate, bytes copied per request, cost per 1M tokens.

Implementation TODOs (concrete):
- [ ] Prototype host-pinned KV allocator with per-tenant namespaces (Mateo).
- [ ] Add delta-copy path to TRT adapter (Priya).
- [ ] Instrument routing table to expose affinity TTLs and metrics (Ethan).
- [ ] Add chaos tests: simulate backend crash mid-request and verify KV fallback correctness.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc intentionally mixes bench notes and design proposals; aim is to converge on one hybrid policy before producing a formal design doc for review.
- Look especially at the pinned memory safety model and billing implications; that's the biggest infra/legal surface.

Slack threads / refs: #runtime-kv-affinity, #trt-integration, + links above.

Unresolved decision choices for product:
- Should we expose an opt-in per-tenant knob to favor low-cost backends at expense of occasional p99 spikes? (Product input requested from solutions_eng).
- Default affinity window size: heavy chats prefer longer affinity; small transactional prompts prefer short. Consider auto-tuning by workload class.

End of scratchpad.
